citations.verbatim_quote: TABLE II. NUMERALS. [Hebrew Fem.:] One Achath, Two Shetayim, Three Shalosh, Four Arbang, Five Chamesh, Six Shesh, Seven Shebang, Eight Shemoneh, Nine Teshang, Ten Nges-reh. | [Aguilar 1853 p. 66:] a place afterwards called Beer-Shebang, or Well of the Oath | [Barrère & Leland 1890 II:226:] and that the word shebang, in Hebrew, means seven.

citations.analysis_notes: Across 183 pre-1862 IA volumes matching `"shebang"`, over a dozen 1795–1857 theological, classical, and ethnographic books (including Jarvis 1820 *Religion of the Indian Tribes of North America* p. 72 leaf 77, Xenophon 1832 leaf 286, Leeser 1834, De Sola 1844, Aguilar 1853 *Women of Israel* p. 66 leaf 69 `Beer-Shebang`, and Davis 1857 *Magic Staff* leaf 346) genuinely print literal `Shebang`/`shebang` in clear English type! Jarvis (1820) is doubly deceptive because its Native American title makes `Shebang` look like an American frontier Algonquian/Iroquois word. Even better, this discovery solves the forgotten riddle in Barrère & Leland (1890, Vol. II, pp. 225–226 leaves 236–237), which quoted a humorous verse (*The Story of Mr. Scroper, Architect*) claiming that a shanty has seven board-surfaces `'and that the word shebang, in Hebrew, means seven... applied to any shanty where they play at seven-up'` — a witty learned pun on Sephardic/grammar-book `shebang` ('seven'), not the historical origin of the American slang word!

XLVII, p. 326, plus page running header '"CHARTERED SHEBANG."'), where Virginia City rough Scotty Briggs charters an omnibus/carriage for Buck Fanshaw's funeral ('I want this shebang all day'). Demonstrates the classic vehicular extension ('carriage, omnibus, contraption') falsely misattributed by later folk etymologists to French char-à-bancs—a hypothesis chronologically refuted by 20 prior years (1852-1871) of tavern, shanty, camp-hut, and collective 'whole chebang/shebang' attestations before the first vehicular use! (Compare also Twain's Dec. 28, 1869 letter to publisher Elisha Bliss: 'believe the chebang will be a success', Mark Twain's Letters, Vol. 3, p. 432.)

citations.linguistic_note: Falsified Schele De Vere (1872) myth: Confederate Louisiana French cabane (/kaban/, 'hut') transmitted across Civil War picket lines
citations.analysis_notes: Primary scan inspection of Schele De Vere (1872 `americanismsengl00scheuoft`) locates his famous conjecture on p. 284 (leaf 289, indexed on p. 680 leaf 686; note Abbyy OCR misread italic *cabane* as `calane`). citations.verbatim_quote: Shebang. A strange word that had its origin during the late civil war. It is applied alike to a room, a shop, or a hut, a tent, a cabin; an engine-house. "Many a poor fellow," says an old soldier, "who enlisted to do hard fighting, lost the number of his mess, and was carried out from his shebang to his long home." — Overland Monthly, for March, 1871.

citations.verbatim_quote: Shebeen or sheebeen; an unlicensed public-house or alehouse where spirits are sold on the sly. (Used all over Ireland.) Irish síbín, same sound and meaning.
citations.linguistic_note: Hiberno-English diminutive suffix -een (< Irish -ín: southern stressed [-ˈiːn] vs. northern unstressed [-ɪn]) in shebeen, transmitted into Mid-Atlantic/New York Irish-American vernacular
citations.analysis_notes: Joyce (1910) provides the exact dialectological key to the vowel/coda remodeling of `shebeen` -> `shebang`: on pp. 90–91 (leaves 104–105), Joyce notes that Irish diminutive `-ín` is pronounced long and stressed `(-een)` `[-ˈiːn]` in southern Ireland (`shebeen` `/ʃɪˈbiːn/`), keeping oxytonic final stress, whereas in northern Ireland it is shortened `(-in)` `[-ɪn]`. On p. 89 Joyce also cites New York Irish-American balladry (`'Shanahan's Ould Shebeen,' New York`). In 1840s–1850s American urban/frontier contact slang, oxytonic `shebeen` (`[ʃəˈbiːn ~ ʃəˈbɪn]`) underwent (a) expressive suffix substitution onto native English intensive `-bang` (`[-ˈbæŋ]`, cf. `CERT-2000-305` `slam-bang` & 1849 `che-bang!`) and (b) hypercorrect `-in -> -ing` velar nasalization + vowel lowering in lively b'hoy/tavern slang, while retaining initial sibilant/affricate variation (`/ʃ/ ~ /tʃ/` in 1852/1854 `Chebang`) and oxytonic stress (`/ʃəˈbæŋ/`).
